summaries.information_need: A researcher wants an overview of the stylized facts of asset returns established across many markets and instruments using non-parametric and semi-parametric statistical methods, together with the basic notation for log returns at a given time scale that underlies the rest of the empirical analysis.

A researcher wants to understand what qualifies as a stylized empirical fact in the study of asset returns, namely a qualitative statistical property common across a wide range of markets, instruments, and time periods, together with the observation that such facts are constraining enough that few stochastic processes can reproduce all of them simultaneously.

A researcher wants the catalogue of stylized statistical properties of returns observed across asset classes, including near-absence of linear autocorrelation, heavy-tailed unconditional distributions, gain-loss asymmetry, aggregational Gaussianity at coarser time scales, volatility clustering, and slow-decaying dependence in absolute returns, along with several other regularities such as intermittency and the leverage effect.

A researcher wants to understand the stationarity hypothesis underlying statistical analysis of asset returns, why it cannot simply be assumed to hold in calendar time given seasonality effects, together with the related but distinct requirement of ergodicity needed for sample averages to converge to their theoretical expectations, and the further complication that finite-sample estimator behavior may differ sharply from asymptotic theory.

A researcher wants to know how the kurtosis of return distribution is used to quantify deviation from the Gaussian benchmark for high-frequency price changes, together with representative empirical kurtosis values reported across different asset classes and the resulting conclusion that a realistic parametric model needs at least four parameters to capture location, scale, tail decay, and asymmetry.
summaries.answer_type: distributional measure with parametric modeling implication

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants tail index estimation methodology based on examining how sample moments behave as sample size grows, distinguishing a finite theoretical moment that settles down from an infinite one that continues to fluctuate erratically, together with the empirical finding that variance appears finite while higher-order moments remain numerically unstable.

A researcher wants extreme value theory applied to asset returns, including the limit theorem characterizing the distribution of normalized maxima for independent sequences, the block-method maximum likelihood procedure for estimating the shape parameter, and the resulting empirical evidence that returns fall in the heavy-tailed domain of attraction relevant for value-at-risk calculation.
summaries.answer_type: methodology specification with empirical tail evidence

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to understand the absence of linear autocorrelation in asset returns beyond very short intraday lags, often cited as support for the efficient market hypothesis, together with the exception of negative autocorrelation at the shortest lags attributed to the bid-ask bounce and mean reversion at the tick level.

A researcher wants to understand volatility clustering as revealed by significant positive autocorrelation in absolute and squared returns despite the absence of linear correlation in returns themselves, together with related nonlinear dependence measures such as the leverage effect, and the resulting decomposition of returns into a white noise term multiplied by a time-varying volatility factor.
summaries.answer_type: empirical dependence property with model decomposition

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know why sample ACF reliability is questionable for heavy-tailed nonlinear return series, since an infinite fourth moment slows the convergence rate and widens confidence bands for both the returns and their squares, together with evidence that even standard GARCH models can produce unreliable autocorrelation estimates of squared residuals.

A researcher wants to know how the covariance matrix of returns can be decomposed into individual volatilities and a correlation matrix, together with random matrix theory evidence that most of its eigenvalues carry no information beyond a random noise benchmark, which raises doubts about naive covariance-based portfolio optimization and supports low-dimensional factor models.
summaries.answer_type: empirical eigenvalue analysis with modeling implication

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to understand correlation of extreme returns as a more relevant dependence measure than ordinary covariance for portfolio diversification during large market moves, expressed as the conditional probability of a large loss in one asset given a large loss in another, together with the observation that assets may exhibit extremal dependence even when their covariance is zero.

A researcher wants the definition of Hölder regularity of price paths through the local Hölder exponent, a mathematical measure of local smoothness of a sample trajectory, together with the observation that this exponent generally varies from one sample path to another for a stochastic process, except for a few notable cases such as fractional Brownian motion.

A researcher wants the definition of the singularity spectrum as a more stable statistical alternative to the sample-path-dependent local Hölder exponent, together with the multifractal formalism that recovers this spectrum from the scaling behavior of sample moments through a Legendre transform of the scaling exponent.

An analyst wants empirical evidence for a universal singularity spectrum shape across many different assets and markets, resembling an inverted parabola with a maximum matching the Hurst exponent reported by other long-range dependence estimators, together with caveats about the reliability of this method in finite samples and the risk of detecting spurious multifractality in non-multifractal data.
